claims.text: People work for income to meet living needs, security, social contact, recognition, achievement and opportunities to develop their abilities. Different people place different weight on these rewards, and priorities can change. Work can support needs without satisfying all of them: a well-paid job may be insecure or isolating. Job security means confidence that employment will continue. Social security concerns protection or benefits against specified risks, rather than simply keeping the same job. Do not substitute one meaning for the other. An employer choosing a motivation approach needs evidence of staff needs, not an assumption that everyone wants the same thing.

claims.text: Taylor emphasises financial incentives and systematic organisation of work. Maslow describes a hierarchy of physiological, safety, social, esteem and self-actualisation needs. Herzberg distinguishes hygiene or maintenance factors that prevent dissatisfaction from motivators within the work itself. These theories suggest different reasons for behaviour and different responses. Pay and safe conditions matter, but they may not provide achievement, recognition or responsibility. Use the theory that explains the stated problem, identify its limits and assess the workforce rather than mixing categories from different theorists. Needs need not follow a rigid identical order for every person. A manager should investigate and review the response instead of treating a theory as proof that one measure will motivate everyone.

claims.text: Fictional Nela Repairs pays adequately and provides secure conditions, but experienced technicians complain that repetitive work gives them no responsibility or recognition. Choose job improvement with staff consultation; basic pay still matters if later evidence shows it is inadequate.

claims.text: Taylor’s scientific-management approach examines tasks systematically, seeks an efficient method, selects suitable workers and links financial reward to output. Piece-rate pay can reward additional acceptable units, making a clear effort–earnings link where output is measurable and workers can influence it. The approach gives money a central role rather than explaining motivation through a hierarchy of needs. Its limits include neglecting social needs and job satisfaction, and encouraging speed at the expense of quality or safety if targets are poorly designed. It suits some repetitive measurable work better than complex team services where individual output is difficult to attribute.

claims.text: Maslow’s hierarchy identifies physiological needs such as basic living requirements, safety needs such as secure and safe work, social needs such as belonging, esteem needs such as recognition and self-actualisation through developing potential. Pay can help basic needs, secure conditions support safety, team relationships support social needs, praise can support esteem and challenging opportunities can support development. The model suggests unmet needs influence motivation, with lower needs commonly receiving attention before higher ones. Do not assume every worker follows an identical fixed sequence or stops valuing money after one need is met. Managers need to identify which needs matter in the particular case.

claims.text: Herzberg distinguishes hygiene or maintenance factors, including pay, conditions, supervision and policies, from motivators such as achievement, recognition, responsibility, advancement and the work itself. Poor hygiene factors can create dissatisfaction; putting them right can remove that dissatisfaction without necessarily producing lasting motivation. Motivators concern positive satisfaction from meaningful work. Job enrichment can add genuine responsibility and challenge rather than merely more repetitive tasks. The model does not justify ignoring wages or claiming that every employee responds identically. Diagnose the actual complaint and avoid labelling Maslow’s hierarchy or Taylor’s output incentives as Herzberg’s categories.
